title: Embedded Systems & IoT
tagline: Frugal engineering — the nervous system that senses and reacts, built to work in the field, not the lab.

intro.text: Every component choice in this chapter is one that works fine on a bench in an air-conditioned lab and fails in a metal box on a wall in Nagpur in May. The failures are predictable, which means they are preventable at the selection stage and expensive at every stage after.

blocks.text: Nominal is 230 V at 50 Hz. Real supply in many places swings far wider — sagging under load in the evening, spiking when a large motor nearby switches off, and dropping out entirely without warning. Brownout, not surge, is what kills Indian embedded devices. A supply that sags to 150 V leaves the SMPS producing a drooping rail, and an MCU running at 2.4 V does not stop - it does something RANDOM, like writing garbage to flash. Use a certified isolated SMPS module. A student building their own mains supply is spending a week to produce something less safe than a ₹250 part

topics.title: Heat, and the component that always dies first

blocks.text: The electrolytic capacitor arithmetic — do this once and you will never buy an 85 °C part again Electrolytic capacitor life roughly halves for every 10 °C above its rated temperature, and doubles for every 10 °C below. The rule is L = L₀ × 2^((T_rated − T_actual)/10). Take a sealed enclosure on a wall in an Indian summer: 42 °C ambient, plus internal rise, gives roughly 65 °C inside. A 2000-hour part rated at 85 °C gives 2000 × 2² = 8,000 hours — under eleven months. The same 2000-hour part rated at 105 °C gives 2000 × 2⁴ = 32,000 hours — about three and a half years. That is a four-fold difference in product life for a component that costs a few rupees more. Specify 105 °C electrolytics in anything that will sit in an Indian enclosure, or use solid polymer or ceramic where the capacitance allows.

• Choose sealed-with-a-heatsink over vented-with-a-fan. A vent is a dust entrance and a fan is a moving part that fails. Conduct heat to an external surface instead — an aluminium plate or the enclosure wall itself.
• IP54 is enough indoors; IP65 outdoors; IP67 only where submersion is credible. And note that an IP65 enclosure with an unsealed cable gland is not IP65. The gland is the part people get wrong.

• Conformal-coat the board for humid or coastal deployments. Acrylic is easiest to apply and to rework; silicone flexes and handles heat; polyurethane is toughest and hardest to repair. Mask the connectors and the antenna before coating.

• Breathe, do not seal absolutely. A fully sealed box heats in the sun, cools at night, and pulls in humid air through any imperfection — which then condenses inside. A Gore-type vent membrane equalises pressure while blocking water and dust, and costs very little.
• Put the drain at the bottom. Assume water will get in. A small weep hole at the lowest point turns a flooded enclosure into a damp one.
• Mount cable entries facing down, with a drip loop before them, so water runs away from the gland rather than into it.

topics.title: Connectivity — and the 2G problem you must know about

blocks.text: Read this before you buy a SIM800L The SIM800L is the cheapest and most documented cellular module in the Indian maker ecosystem, and it is 2G only. That matters more every year:

Jio has never operated a 2G network at all — it is 4G/VoLTE only, so a SIM800L will never register on a Jio SIM, no matter what you do. Airtel still runs 2G but has shut it down across several circles and metro areas. Vi has signalled a partial shutdown in the 2026–27 window. BSNL and rural 2G on the 900 MHz band are expected to persist for some years, but nobody will guarantee how many.

Practical rule: SIM800L is fine to learn AT commands on, and fine for a semester project you will dismantle. For anything intended to run for two or three years, specify a 4G Cat-1 module — the A7670E covers the Indian LTE bands (B3, B5, B8, B40, B41), the A7670G adds GNSS so one module does both connectivity and location, and the SIM7080G gives you LTE Cat-M1 and NB-IoT for low-power work. The AT command set is close enough that migration is minor.

An hour, and it will save you a re-spin.
1 Write the deployment environment down as numbers: worst ambient temperature, whether it is sealed, whether there is mains, whether there is dust or rain.
2 Pick a microcontroller and check its temperature grade against your worst case. Most hobby boards are commercial grade.

5 Write one sentence for each of the four stressors saying what you have done about it. ‘Nothing yet’ is a valid answer and becomes your task list.

intro.text: The workflow exists to make mistakes cheap. A error caught in the schematic costs minutes; the same error caught after the boards arrive costs three weeks and a re-spin. Every stage below has a review gate for exactly that reason.

THE RULE: never skip a gate because you are confident. Confidence is exactly the state in which people order 20 boards with a swapped footprint.
Stages 1 and 2 take an afternoon and prevent most re-spins. Students skip straight to stage 3 and pay for it at stage 5
• Draw the power tree first, as a separate sheet. Every source, every regulator, every rail, with the expected current on each. If you cannot total the current, you cannot choose the regulator.

• One decoupling capacitor per supply pin, 100 nF, placed in the layout right at the pin — not merely present in the schematic. Add bulk capacitance where current is bursty (a radio needs far more than the datasheet minimum; see §4.4).
• Name every net. SDA, VBAT, MOTOR_EN. Unnamed nets become unreadable in three weeks and unreviewable by anyone else.
• Add test points on every rail and every critical signal. A 1 mm pad costs nothing at design time and is the difference between debugging in ten minutes and soldering wires onto a QFN pin.

• Fit 0 Ω links and DNP footprints at your uncertainties. Not sure whether you need a pull-up, a filter or that extra series resistor? Put the footprint down, populate it if needed. A footprint you did not use costs nothing; one you did not place costs a re-spin.
• Bring out a debug header — UART at minimum, SWD/JTAG if your MCU supports it. Every board you will ever want to debug in the field is one you did not put a header on.
• Get it reviewed by a human. Print it, hand it to someone, and make them trace the power path and one signal path aloud. Most fatal errors are found in that twenty minutes.

PROTOCOL — Board bring-up — follow in order, do not skip ahead

STEP 0 VISUAL, before any power Inspect every solder joint under magnification. Look for bridges, tombstoned parts, wrong orientation on every polarised component. Check the diode and electrolytic polarity marks against the BOM. Ten minutes here saves a destroyed board.

STEP 1 CONTINUITY, with the board unpowered Measure resistance from every rail to ground. A dead short on 3V3-to-GND means STOP - find it before applying power. Expect a few hundred ohms to a few kilohms, not zero.

Use a bench supply with the current limit set LOW - say 100 mA. If you do not have one, a USB power bank through an ammeter, or a resistor in series, is a frugal substitute. Apply power. Watch the current. It should be small and stable. If the limit trips, you have found a fault without releasing smoke.
Every regulator output, with a meter, against the schematic. Write the measured values on a printout of the power tree. Do not proceed until every rail is within tolerance.
STEP 4 CURRENT DRAW vs PREDICTION Compare against your chapter 3 estimate. A large discrepancy is information: something is on that should not be, or vice versa.

STEP 5 PROGRAM IT - the smallest possible program Blink an LED. Nothing else. This proves power, clock, reset and the programming interface all work. If the blink fails, the problem is in those four things, not in your application.

UART first (so you can print). Then I2C - scan the bus and confirm every expected address responds. Then each sensor. Then the radio, last, because it is the biggest current draw and the most likely to expose a power problem.
STEP 7 ONLY NOW run the application firmware. Step 2 is the one that saves boards. A current-limited supply turns ‘I destroyed the prototype’ into ‘I found a short in thirty seconds’.

topics.title: Firmware that survives being left alone

blocks.text: Firmware on your desk gets restarted whenever it misbehaves. Firmware in a field does not. Six structural decisions separate code that runs for a month unattended from code that needs someone to power-cycle it every Tuesday.

• Enable the watchdog, and feed it in exactly one place. A watchdog fed from several places — or worse, from inside an interrupt — will happily keep a hung program alive. Feed it once, at the top of the main loop, only after the loop has completed a full pass.

• No blocking calls anywhere in the main path. Not delay(), not a synchronous network call without a timeout, not a while loop waiting for a sensor that may never answer. Every wait needs a timeout and a path for what happens when it expires.

• Define fail-safe defaults explicitly. What does the device do when the sensor reads out of range, when the server is unreachable, when the clock is wrong, when the battery is nearly flat? Write the answer down for each. Undefined behaviour in the field means whatever the last programmer happened to leave in a variable.

• Bounds-check everything that comes from outside — sensor readings, downlink commands, stored configuration. A sensor returning 0xFFFF because its bus glitched should be rejected as invalid, not logged as a real reading and averaged into your data.

• Persist what must survive a reset, and nothing more. Cumulative counters, sequence numbers and configuration go in flash or RTC memory; write them rarely and atomically, because a power cut mid-write is how flash gets corrupted.
• Report your firmware version in every heartbeat. When twenty units are deployed and three behave oddly, the first question is always which build they are running — and you will not remember.

• Decide about over-the-air updates deliberately. OTA adds real risk: a bad update can brick every unit at once. It also saves a day of travel per site visit. If you implement it, keep a known-good fallback image and roll out to one unit before all of them.

topics.title: The enclosure, which is part of the electronics

blocks.text: The box is not packaging. It sets your thermal performance, your ingress rating, your antenna performance and whether anyone can service the device — and it is routinely designed last, after the PCB outline is already fixed, which is how boards end up not fitting.

• Choose the enclosure before you finalise the PCB outline. Buy the actual box, measure it, and draw the board to fit — including standoff positions, connector cutout heights and the lid’s internal ribs, which are what actually collide with your tall capacitors.

• Metal is a Faraday cage. A metal enclosure will destroy your Wi-Fi, LoRa or cellular link. Use ABS or polycarbonate, or bring an external antenna outside on a pigtail. Polycarbonate survives UV far better than ABS outdoors.

• Plan the thermal path. A sealed box with a regulator dissipating a watt needs somewhere to send it: a metal plate bonded to the enclosure wall, or a thermal pad to a heatsink on the outside. Do not vent — see §1.3.
• Cable entries face down, with a drip loop. Glands sized to the cable, tightened properly. An oversized gland on a thin cable seals nothing.

• Design for the tenth unit, not the first. Can you assemble it in five minutes? Can you open it in the field without losing screws in the grass? Captive screws and a hinged lid are worth the extra rupees.
• Prototype in cardboard first. A full-size cardboard mock-up of the enclosure, with the PCB inside, catches connector clashes and cable-routing problems in twenty minutes and costs nothing.
BUILD THIS — Take one simple board through the whole workflow
Two to three weeks, most of it waiting for parts and boards.
1 Design something deliberately simple: an ESP32, a regulator, one sensor, a connector, and test points. The goal is the process, not the product.
2 Draw the power tree as its own sheet with the current on every rail.
3 Get the schematic reviewed by another person who traces the power path aloud.
4 Run the DFM check against your chosen fab’s actual design rules — they differ, and the cheap options have looser minimums.
5 Order boards, a stencil, and 30% extra passives. Order the parts first, so they arrive before the boards do.
6 Bring it up with the §2.4 procedure and write down the measured value of every rail. Keep that sheet — it becomes the reference when a later board misbehaves.

intro.text: Battery life is not a firmware optimisation applied at the end. It is a budget you compute at the start, in milliamp-hours per day, and then defend against every design decision that follows.

topics.title: Peak current, and why your device resets when it transmits

blocks.text: A cellular module transmits in bursts that can pull two amps for a couple of milliseconds. Your battery has internal resistance; your wiring has resistance; your regulator has a response time. The voltage at the module dips, and if it dips far enough your microcontroller browns out and resets — which is why so many first GSM projects reboot every time they try to send.
A tired 18650 has an internal resistance around 150 mOhm. Add 100 mOhm of thin wire and a connector. V_dip = I x R = 2 A x 0.25 Ohm = 0.5 V

A cell at 3.7 V sags to 3.2 V during the burst. The SIM800L needs at least 3.4 V. It resets, or it fails to register, or it corrupts the AT command mid-sequence - and the fault is intermittent, which is the worst kind.

THE FIXES, in order of effectiveness 1. BULK CAPACITANCE right at the module's power pins. 1000-2200 uF low-ESR electrolytic, PLUS a 100 nF ceramic. The cap supplies the burst; the battery recharges it between bursts. This single component fixes most GSM instability. 2. SHORT, THICK POWER WIRING to the module. At 2 A, 100 mm of thin jumper wire is a meaningful resistance. Do not power a GSM module through a breadboard. 3. A HEALTHY CELL, or a supercapacitor in parallel for pulse support. 4. SEPARATE the MCU supply from the module supply, or at minimum give the MCU its own bulk cap and a decent brownout threshold, so a module dip cannot reset your controller.
Power a GSM module from a microcontroller board's 3V3 or 5V pin. Those regulators supply 150-300 mA. The module needs 2 A. This is the single most common cause of "my SIM800L does not work".
If a cellular project behaves erratically, assume power before you assume firmware. It is power roughly nine times out of ten

• The problem: a multimeter in current mode has a burden voltage — it drops volts across its own shunt — and it cannot follow a device that swings between 20 µA and 200 mA. Switch ranges mid-measurement and many meters momentarily open the circuit, resetting your device.

• Frugal method 1 — the capacitor discharge test. Charge a known capacitor (say 1 F supercap or a large electrolytic) to a known voltage, run the device from it alone, and time the voltage drop. I_avg = C × ΔV / Δt. Crude, but it measures average current over a full duty cycle, which is exactly what your budget needs.

• Frugal method 2 — the long run. Fully charge a battery of known capacity, run the device until it dies, and divide. It takes days and it is the most honest number you will get, because it includes self-discharge, temperature and everything you forgot.

• Frugal method 3 — shunt plus multimeter in volts mode. Put a 1 Ω or 10 Ω resistor in the supply line and measure the voltage across it. No range switching, no burden-voltage surprise. 10 Ω gives 10 mV per milliamp — readable on any meter.

• If you can borrow one thing, borrow a dedicated current profiler or a USB power analyser. But do not let its absence stop you: method 2 with a stopwatch and a calendar beats a precise instrument you do not have.

- panels get dusty and are rarely cleaned; output falls over a season - cells age and lose capacity, and a node should last years - the minimum practical panel and cell you can actually buy are already bigger than the calculation demands - the difference between a 1 W and a 5 W panel is about Rs 200, and margin is cheap insurance against the thing you forgot

If your node genuinely NEEDS a 5 W panel, your load is roughly a hundred times what a well-designed node draws. Do not buy a bigger panel - go and find the leak. It will be one of: a sensor left powered between readings (5.4) a radio sleeping instead of powered off (3.2) a dev board's USB-serial chip and power LED (3.2) a linear regulator with high quiescent current Oversizing the panel to cover a leak is the most expensive way to fix a firmware bug.

intro.text: The cheapest, safest and most accurate way to measure a building’s energy consumption is not to measure it at all — it is to read the meter the utility already installed and calibrated, by counting the light it flashes.

topics.title: Two approaches, and why we pick the second

Unless you specifically need per-circuit breakdown, pulse counting wins on every axis that matters. It is the frugal-engineering answer: let the calibrated instrument that already exists do the hard part.
The safety argument, stated plainly

Almost every Indian electronic meter has a red calibration LED that pulses at a rate printed on its faceplate — commonly 1600 or 3200 impulses per kWh, sometimes 1000. A phototransistor taped over that LED involves no electrical connection to anything. Your circuit is galvanically isolated from mains by an air gap and a plastic window.

Do not open the meter, do not break its seal, and do not tap its terminals. The seal is a legal device and breaking it is a serious matter regardless of the electrical risk. Everything in this project happens outside the meter.
Every pulse represents a FIXED quantity of energy:
energy per pulse (Wh) = 1000 / N where N = impulses per kWh
N = 1000 imp/kWh -> 1.0000 Wh per pulse N = 1600 imp/kWh -> 0.6250 Wh per pulse N = 3200 imp/kWh -> 0.3125 Wh per pulse
INSTANTANEOUS POWER, from the time between two pulses:
P (watts) = 3,600,000 / (N x T) T = seconds between pulses
at N = 3200: 200 W -> a pulse every 5.625 s 1000 W -> a pulse every 1.125 s 3000 W -> a pulse every 0.375 s
CUMULATIVE ENERGY is simply the pulse count:
kWh = pulses / N

- Read N off the meter faceplate. Do not assume it. - At low load the interval is long. Below about 100 W you may wait 10 seconds between pulses, so instantaneous power is noisy - average over several pulses before reporting it. - The pulse itself is short (typically 10-100 ms). Sample fast enough or use an interrupt, which is what we do.
One division and one counter. Compare this to the sampling, RMS and power-factor work the CT-clamp route requires

intro.text: Two things kill farm IoT deployments: the probe corrodes away inside a month, and the network drops for a day and the data is gone forever. Both are design decisions, and both are made before you write any firmware.

topics.title: Resistive probes do not work. Use capacitive

blocks.text: The single most important sentence in this chapter The cheap two-prong soil moisture sensor sold everywhere for ₹40 measures resistance by passing current between two exposed metal electrodes. Passing current through damp, ion-rich soil is electrolysis. The electrodes oxidise and erode, the readings drift upward as they do, and within a few weeks — sometimes days in fertilised soil — the probe is both physically eaten and numerically meaningless. A capacitive probe measures the dielectric constant of the surrounding soil through an insulating coating. No exposed metal, no current through the soil, no corrosion. It costs ₹150–400 instead of ₹40 and it is the difference between a project and a demonstration. One caveat worth knowing: many cheap ‘capacitive’ boards have exposed via barrels or an unsealed top edge. Seal the top of the board and the cable entry with epoxy before it goes in the ground, whatever the seller claims.

topics.title: Calibration — what the number actually means

blocks.text: A capacitive probe gives you an ADC count, not a moisture percentage. The mapping from one to the other depends on your soil — clay, loam and sand with identical water content read differently, and salinity shifts it again. Two levels of calibration, and you should do at least the first:
LEVEL 1 - TWO-POINT, takes ten minutes, gives relative moisture
raw_dry = reading in air (or in oven-dried soil) raw_wet = reading fully submerged in water moisture% = 100 x (raw_dry - raw) / (raw_dry - raw_wet)
Good enough for "is it drier than yesterday" and for threshold irrigation triggers. NOT a volumetric water content, and do not report it as one.
LEVEL 2 - GRAVIMETRIC, the frugal way to get real numbers You need a kitchen scale (0.1 g) and an oven or a hot plate.
1. Take a soil sample from beside the probe. Note the probe reading.
2. Weigh the wet sample. -> W_wet
3. Dry it thoroughly - 105 C for 24 h, or until the mass stops
falling on repeated weighings.
4. Weigh it dry. -> W_dry
gravimetric water content = (W_wet - W_dry) / W_dry
5. Repeat across 5-6 different moisture levels, from nearly dry to saturated, recording the probe reading each time.
6. Fit a curve (usually close to linear over the useful range).
Now your ADC count maps to a real, defensible water content FOR THAT SOIL. Redo it if you move to a different field.
Not a percentage. Two thresholds:
FIELD CAPACITY - the soil holds all it can against gravity.
Irrigating past this wastes water and leaches
nutrients.
REFILL POINT - the level at which the crop starts to suffer.
This is the trigger to irrigate.
Establish these two numbers with the farmer, in the field, and report
against them. "Moisture 34%" means nothing to anyone. "Below refill
point, irrigate today" is a decision.
Level 1 plus the two thresholds is a genuinely useful product. Level 2 is what makes your report defensible to an agronomist

modules.title: Project 3 — Wearable Fall Detection and Location

intro.text: A fall detector that cries wolf is worse than no detector at all, because within a fortnight nobody responds to it. The engineering problem is not detecting falls — it is not detecting everything else.

topics.title: Before the engineering: this device watches a person

blocks.text: Design the safety function. Refuse the surveillance function.

A device worn by a worker that knows where they are and whether they are moving is a safety device and a surveillance device built from identical hardware. Which one it becomes is decided by design choices, not by intentions — and function creep is the default outcome unless you design against it.

What honest design looks like here: location resolved to a zone, not a coordinate, because a rescuer needs to know which bay to run to and nobody needs to know which machine someone stood at for how long. Data retained for days, not years, with automatic deletion. No continuous location logging — store location only when an alarm fires. No productivity metrics, no idle-time reports, no per-worker dashboards, and say so in writing.

And the part engineers skip: the workers wearing it should be told what it records, what it does not, who can see it, and how long it is kept — in their language — before deployment, not after. A device introduced without that conversation gets left in a locker, which means it protects nobody. Consent is not only an ethical requirement here; it is the thing that makes the safety function work at all.

A simple ‘acceleration exceeded 3 g’ threshold produces false alarms constantly — setting the device down hard, a dropped tool, jumping off a step. A real fall has a signature in sequence, and requiring all four phases in order removes most false positives at no cost in sensitivity.

FallState st = NORMAL;
uint32_t tState = 0;

float mag = sqrtf(ax*ax + ay*ay + az*az); // in g
uint32_t now = millis();
switch (st) {
case NORMAL:
pitchBefore = estimatePitch(ax, ay, az); // rolling reference
if (mag < FREEFALL_G) { st = FREEFALL; tState = now; }
break;
case FREEFALL:
if (mag > IMPACT_G && (now - tState) > FREEFALL_MIN_MS) {

startCancelWindow(); }

break;

else if ((now - tState) > CANCEL_MS) { st = ALARM; raiseAlarm(); }
break;
case ALARM: if (cancelPressed()) st = NORMAL; break;

topics.title: Location: GPS does not work where the worker is

blocks.text: The assumption that breaks this project GPS needs sky. Inside a factory shed with a metal roof, under a gantry, in a basement or a warehouse aisle, a GPS module will either report nothing or — worse — report a stale fix from the last time it saw sky, sending rescuers to the car park. For an indoor industrial deployment, use BLE beacons. Place inexpensive battery beacons at known points — one per bay, per line, per floor. The wearable records the strongest beacon it can hear and reports that zone. It is coarse, it is cheap, it works through people and machinery, it draws almost no power, and ‘Bay 4, Line 2’ is exactly what a rescuer needs. Precision beyond the zone is not useful to a rescuer and is useful to a surveillance system — see §6.1. Keep GPS only if the work is genuinely outdoors, and then use a module with GNSS built into the cellular modem (the A7670G) rather than a second chip.

topics.title: Wearing it, powering it, keeping it alive

blocks.text: • Mount position changes everything. Waist or belt is the standard for fall detection because it approximates the body’s centre of mass. A wrist-worn device sees enormous acceleration from ordinary arm movement and is far harder to tune. If you must use the wrist, expect to raise thresholds and rely more heavily on the orientation and stillness stages.

• Budget for the alarm, not the average. The device sleeps most of the time, wakes on IMU motion interrupt, and only powers the radio when something happens. Use the IMU’s own wake-on-motion feature so the MCU is not sampling continuously.

• Charging discipline is a design problem. A device that needs daily charging will be flat when it matters. Aim for a week, use a magnetic or drop-in charger rather than a fiddly connector, and make the charge state visible at a glance from across a room.

• Make it comfortable or it will not be worn. Weight, strap, sharp corners, heat against skin. A device in a locker has a detection rate of zero, and this is the most common failure mode of worker wearables — not technical, human.

• Test tampering honestly. If the device is uncomfortable or distrusted, some people will leave it on a bench. Detecting ‘not being worn’ (via skin temperature or a total absence of motion) is legitimate safety engineering — but report it as ‘device not worn’ to the safety officer, not as an attendance metric to a supervisor. That distinction is the whole of §6.1 in one design decision.

Stage 3 is the honest one. Reporting sensitivity without reporting the false alarm rate is the standard way fall-detection projects overstate themselves.

BUILD THIS — Build it, and report both numbers Three weekends. The deliverable is a labelled dataset and two percentages. 1 Get the ethics conversation done first: write the one-page statement from §6.1 covering what is recorded, what is not, who

reflects reality. 4 Implement the five-stage algorithm and the cancel window. Tune offline against the dataset. 5 Report detection rate and false alarms per 100 non-fall events. Both numbers, together, always. 6 Deploy the beacons and confirm zone accuracy from the corners of each zone, which is where it fails.

The frugal strategy that actually works: prototype from the local market or an Indian retailer so you are never blocked; place one consolidated Chinese order for the parts you now know you need, in production quantity, while you continue developing; and buy anything critical or hard to authenticate from an authorised distributor regardless of price. Mixing routes deliberately beats optimising for any one of them.

topics.title: Counterfeits, and how to catch them

blocks.text: Assume the cheapest listing is the fake one Batteries are the worst category. A cell marked ‘9800 mAh’ is a lie: genuine 18650 cells top out around 3500 mAh. Weigh it — a real 3000 mAh 18650 weighs roughly 45–48 g; a counterfeit with a small cell and filler weighs 30–35 g. That single test, with a kitchen scale, catches most of them. USB-serial chips. Counterfeit FTDI FT232 parts have historically been disabled by driver updates. A genuine CH340 costs so little that faking it is pointless — which makes CH340-based boards a safer choice for student work. Sensors. BMP280 relabelled as BME280 (no humidity output, and you will spend a day debugging it) is extremely common. Read the chip ID register: the part tells you what it really is, and your code should check. Microcontrollers. Compare the marking against the manufacturer’s current datasheet. Genuine parts are usually laser-etched with crisp, slightly recessed characters; counterfeits are often printed and rub off with isopropyl alcohol. The general rule: for anything that matters, buy from an authorised distributor and pay the premium. For everything else, verify on arrival — read the ID register, weigh the cell, measure the capacitance, run the part hot for an hour.

The most common silent failure in deployed IoT is a device that stops reporting and is never noticed — because ‘no alerts’ looks exactly like ‘everything is fine’. Send a periodic heartbeat containing battery voltage, uptime, firmware version and signal strength, and alert on its absence. On the cellular advice in §1.4 and §4.4. As of mid-2026, Reliance Jio operates no 2G network at all and never has, so 2G-only modules such as the SIM800L cannot register on a Jio SIM under any circumstances. Airtel continues to run 2G but has withdrawn it across several circles and metro areas; Vi has signalled a partial shutdown in the 2026–27 window; BSNL and rural 900 MHz coverage are expected to persist for some further years without any guarantee. For designs intended to run two years or more, specify a 4G Cat-1 module. Verify the current position before committing to a module — this is moving.

And the habit that matters most. Everything expensive in this guide — the capacitor that died in eleven months, the module that browned out its own controller, the probe that corroded, the two days of readings lost to a network outage, the fall detector nobody trusted — was a decision made early and discovered late. The workflow in Chapter 2 exists to move that discovery earlier, and the abuse testing in Chapter 7 exists to move it earlier still. Break your own device on purpose, on a bench, on a Tuesday afternoon. It is much cheaper than finding out in a field in July.
